body:
Hello, thank you for reading my comment below:
The White House is a National Historic Landmark, owned by the American people and home to presidents
since 1800. The current president at any given time is not the owner of the property or the structures
thereon; the president is a temporary tenant whose interventions are limited by law and by respect for the
people of the United States. The demolition of the historic East Wing without review, without permits was
and is a violation of the law. I would add that it is also a violation of the trust of the American people who
were given zero opportunity to comment on what *should have been* presented as a proposal.
I urge the National Capital Planning Commission to require reconstruction of the East Wing in keeping with
its historic design and size. Anything constructed on the demolition site must be compatible in form and
subordinate in scale to the original structure of the Executive Mansion. Thank you for your attention to this
matter.

We are allegedly a country governed by the Rule of Law. We have laws and procedures in place that impact
all citizens, residents, and visitors to our country. We have three branches of government to provide a
system of checks and balances.

place, bypasses Congress, or Congressional Oversight, and / or ignores the Courts (Supreme or otherwise),
we no longer are a country governed by the Rule of Law.

Congress. Nothing was presented to the National Historic Trust. This was an entirely illegal act, from start to
finish.
The East Wing needs to be restored - in full - and NOT at the taxpayers expense. The current First Family
should be financially responsible for the restoration as they are responsible for bypassing the systems in
place which would have prevented this from ever happening in the first place.
Thank you for taking the time to read my comments.
Regards,
Polly Hall

body:
Thank you for this opportunity to register my dissatisfaction with the proposed "East Wing Modernization
Project." The destruction of the East Wing itself was initiated without proper authorization, building
permits, or design reviews. This is yet another attempt on the part of the current President to remove any
historical references to former White House occupants and as such, is a vanity project.
A sitting President of the United States of America has taken it upon himself to arbitrarily demolish a
fundamental structural element of the People's House without having first sought permission and review
under the lawful requirements for such extensive changes. As far as I know, there is no record of what
became of everything that was contained in the East Wing, so we only have photographic evidence that any
of it even existed before the demolition.
I urge you to put an immediate halt to any further demolition or "modernization" efforts to the White
House proposed by this Administration or President -- the People's House is not a private property of the
President. I want you to demand that the East Wing be fully restored, down to the last brick, floorboard,
and window pane.

subject: Written Comments
name: Judy Scott
body:
The White House is a National Historic Landmark and a National Park, owned by the American people and
home to presidents since 1800. The current president at any given time is not the owner of the property or
the structures thereon; the president is a temporary tenant whose interventions are limited by law and by
respect for the people of the United States.
The demolition of the historic East Wing without review, without permits and without Congressional
oversight is clearly a violation of the law. In addition, it is a violation of the trust of the American people
who were given no opportunity to comment on what should have been presented as a proposal and not as
a violent fait accompli.
I urge the National Capital Planning Commission to require reconstruction of the East Wing in keeping with
its historic design and size. Anything constructed on the demolition site going forward must be compatible
in form and subordinate in scale to the original structure of the Executive Mansion.

subject: Written Comments
name: Simon Jacobsen
body:
The proposed ballroom and underground bunker is simply too large for the proportions of the White House
and West Wing. We must keep in mind that the White House is a residential building with offices attached,
so therefore, the architectural language, scale and composition needs to address these factors as they have
in the past. However, the new ballroom project seems to ignore all of these architectural signifiers that are
common in good taste, and the art form of design.
The White House, with its central placement and harmonious composition is being completely dwarfed by
an unintelligent, distasteful look-alike of classical architecture. The new ballroom’s size and proportion if, to
be allowed to be built at all, and it shouldn’t, needs to address the immediate scale of the White House and
the appropriate domestic scale.
The construction of the ballroom should not be allowed to commence because of its poor design, size,
proportion as well as the fact that the White House doesn’t need a bigger ballroom at all.

body:

To the Commissioners and Staff of the National Capital Planning Commission:
I am writing as a concerned citizen to submit formal public comment regarding the ongoing White House
East Wing Modernization Project and the recently disclosed proposal to add a second story to the West
Wing colonnade. I urge the Commission to exercise its full authority and independent oversight role in
evaluating these projects —  both individually and as part of what is increasingly apparent to be a much
larger, undisclosed master plan for the White House campus.
I. Concern for Historical Integrity
The White House is not merely the residence and workplace of the President — it is among the most
historically significant structures in the United States and belongs, in the deepest sense, to the American
people. Its neoclassical design, its symmetrical balance of East and West Wings, and the proportional
relationship of those wings to the original central pavilion represent over two centuries of careful,
deliberate stewardship by every prior administration.
The demolition of the East Wing in October 2025 —  which proceeded without prior public notice, without
approved construction plans on file with this Commission, and without formal review by the Commission of
Fine Arts —  constitutes a serious breach of the historical review processes that have long governed changes
to the White House campus. The destruction of the East Wing was the most significant structural alteration
to the White House since the Truman Balcony in 1948. That prior administrations undertook even far more
modest changes through full and transparent review makes the speed and secrecy of this demolition all the
more troubling.
I echo the concerns raised by NCPC Commissioner Phil Mendelson, who questioned why plans were
presented to this Commission only after demolition was already underway, rendering many design
alternatives moot before they could be meaningfully considered. The logic of presenting a project for
review after irreversible action has been taken is fundamentally at odds with the purpose of this body.
I am further alarmed by the disclosure — offered almost in passing during the January 8, 2026
informational presentation — that the administration is now considering a second-story addition to the
West Wing colonnade. This addition was presented without renderings, without a timeline, and without any
formal plan documents. The architect’s acknowledgment that “anything is possible” regarding future design
changes, combined with vague references to potential alterations to Lafayette Park and visitor screening
areas, strongly suggests that the Commission is being shown only one piece of a far larger transformation
that has never been presented in its entirety.
The Commission must insist on reviewing the full scope of the administration’s vision for the White House
campus before approving any individual component. Piecemeal review of a comprehensive redesign is not
meaningful review — it is the appearance of oversight without its substance.
II. Lack of Congressional Oversight and Appropriate Planning Authority
The scale of the proposed construction — a nearly 90,000-square-foot East Wing ballroom, a two-story East
colonnade, and now a proposed West Wing colonnade addition — represents a transformation of the
People’s House with no meaningful role for the legislative branch of government.
Congress holds the power of the purse, and major alterations to federal properties of this historic
significance have historically involved legislative engagement, if not explicit authorization. The bypassing of
that process here —  justified in part by the claim that demolition falls outside the NCPC’s jurisdiction —
reflects an unnervingly narrow interpretation of accountability. As former NCPC Chair L. Preston Bryant Jr.
has stated publicly, demolition is inherently part of a construction project and should not be artificially
separated to circumvent review.
I urge this Commission to interpret its authority broadly and in the spirit of the laws that created it: to
ensure that federally significant construction in the National Capital region reflects the values, interests,
and input of the public it serves —  not simply the preferences of the current occupant of the building in
question. I also call on this Commission to formally recommend that Congress be provided a full accounting
of the proposed changes and their long-term implications for the White House campus.
III. Transparency of Private Funding
The administration has stated that the East Wing ballroom project will be funded entirely through private
donations, at an estimated cost that has already ballooned from $200 million to upwards of $400 million.
While private philanthropy has played a role in certain White House improvements historically, the scale
and opacity of this arrangement warrant serious scrutiny.
Private funding of public infrastructure on this scale raises fundamental questions: Who are the donors?
What access or influence, if any, do they receive in return? Are their contributions subject to the gift
acceptance rules and disclosure requirements that govern federal transactions? The White House delayed
publishing its donor list until October 22, 2025 — only after public pressure — and the full list of donors
and their affiliations has still not been subject to meaningful independent review.
This Commission, in evaluating the project, should formally request complete and independently verified
disclosure of all funding sources, gift agreements, and any conditions or benefits attached to private
contributions. The American people deserve to know who is paying to reshape the People’s House —  and
why.
IV. Public Accountability and Process
At its core, my concern is about process — and what is lost when process is abandoned in favor of speed.
The legally mandated review processes involving the NCPC, the Commission of Fine Arts, the National Park
Service, and the public comment period exist for good reason. They ensure that changes to irreplaceable
national landmarks are made deliberately, transparently, and with the benefit of expert and public input.
They have guided White House stewardship under every administration since 1792.
Those processes were bypassed here. Demolition began before plans were filed. Trees planted in honor of
presidents Warren G. Harding and Franklin D. Roosevelt were removed without public notice. The
Presidential Emergency Operations Center beneath the East Wing was dismantled. All of this occurred
before this Commission had an opportunity to weigh in.
I respectfully urge the National Capital Planning Commission to:
Require the full scope of all planned and contemplated changes to the White House campus — including
the West Wing colonnade addition, Lafayette Park modifications, and visitor screening changes — to be
presented and reviewed as a comprehensive whole, not in isolated fragments.
Condition any construction approval on complete compliance with all applicable review processes, including
the Commission of Fine Arts and the National Environmental Policy Act, prior to further vertical
construction.
Mandate full public disclosure of all private funding sources, gift agreements, and donor-related conditions
associated with this project.
Formally recommend that appropriate congressional committees be briefed on and given the opportunity
to weigh in on the totality of the proposed changes to the White House campus.
Assert the Commission’s independent role free from undue influence from administration-appointed
members who serve simultaneously on this body and in advocacy roles for the projects under review.
The White House has endured for over two centuries as a symbol of democratic governance, institutional
continuity, and the dignity of the American Republic. Its preservation is not a partisan issue. It is an
American one. I trust this Commission to uphold that responsibility with the seriousness it deserves.
Respectfully submitted,
Angie Swenson
Atlanta, GA

Name: Angie Swenson 
Project Name: East Wing Modernization Project 
Project Number: 8733 
 
To the Commissioners and Staff of the National Capital Planning Commission: 
 
I am writing as a concerned citizen to submit formal public comment regarding the ongoing White House 
East Wing Modernization Project and the recently disclosed proposal to add a second story to the West 
Wing colonnade. I urge the Commission to exercise its full authority and independent oversight role in 
evaluating these projects —  both individually and as part of what is increasingly apparent to be a much 
larger, undisclosed master plan for the White House campus. 
 
 
I. Concern for Historical Integrity 
 
The White House is not merely the residence and workplace of the President — it is among the most 
historically significant structures in the United States and belongs, in the deepest sense, to the American 
people. Its neoclassical design, its symmetrical balance of East and West Wings, and the proportional 
relationship of those wings to the original central pavilion represent over two centuries of careful, 
deliberate stewardship by every prior administration. 
 
The demolition of the East Wing in October 2025 —  which proceeded without prior public notice, without 
approved construction plans on file with this Commission, and without formal review by the Commission of 
Fine Arts —  constitutes a serious breach of the historical review processes that have long governed changes 
to the White House campus. The destruction of the East Wing was the most significant structural alteration 
to the White House since the Truman Balcony in 1948. That prior administrations undertook even far more 
modest changes through full and transparent review makes the speed and secrecy of this demolition all the 
more troubling. 
 
I echo the concerns raised by NCPC Commissioner Phil Mendelson, who questioned why plans were 
presented to this Commission only after demolition was already underway, rendering many design 
alternatives moot before they could be meaningfully considered. The logic of presenting a project for 
review after irreversible action has been taken is fundamentally at odds with the purpose of this body. 
 
I am further alarmed by the disclosure — offered almost in passing during the January 8, 2026 
informational presentation — that the administration is now considering a second-story addition to the 
West Wing colonnade. This addition was presented without renderings, without a timeline, and without any 
formal plan documents. The architect’s acknowledgment that “anything is possible” regarding future design 
changes, combined with vague references to potential alterations to Lafayette Park and visitor screening 
areas, strongly suggests that the Commission is being shown only one piece of a far larger transformation 
that has never been presented in its entirety. 
 
The Commission must insist on reviewing the full scope of the administration’s vision for the White House 
campus before approving any individual component. Piecemeal review of a comprehensive redesign is not 
meaningful review — it is the appearance of oversight without its substance. 
 
 
II. Lack of Congressional Oversight and Appropriate Planning Authority 
 
The scale of the proposed construction — a nearly 90,000-square-foot East Wing ballroom, a two-story East 
colonnade, and now a proposed West Wing colonnade addition — represents a transformation of the 
People’s House with no meaningful role for the legislative branch of government. 
 
Congress holds the power of the purse, and major alterations to federal properties of this historic 
significance have historically involved legislative engagement, if not explicit authorization. The bypassing of 
that process here —  justified in part by the claim that demolition falls outside the NCPC’s jurisdiction — 
reflects an unnervingly narrow interpretation of accountability. As former NCPC Chair L. Preston Bryant Jr. 
has stated publicly, demolition is inherently part of a construction project and should not be artificially 
separated to circumvent review. 
 
I urge this Commission to interpret its authority broadly and in the spirit of the laws that created it: to 
ensure that federally significant construction in the National Capital region reflects the values, interests, 
and input of the public it serves —  not simply the preferences of the current occupant of the building in 
question. I also call on this Commission to formally recommend that Congress be provided a full accounting 
of the proposed changes and their long-term implications for the White House campus. 
 
 
III. Transparency of Private Funding 
 
The administration has stated that the East Wing ballroom project will be funded entirely through private 
donations, at an estimated cost that has already ballooned from $200 million to upwards of $400 million. 
While private philanthropy has played a role in certain White House improvements historically, the scale 
and opacity of this arrangement warrant serious scrutiny. 
 
Private funding of public infrastructure on this scale raises fundamental questions: Who are the donors? 
What access or influence, if any, do they receive in return? Are their contributions subject to the gift 
acceptance rules and disclosure requirements that govern federal transactions? The White House delayed 
publishing its donor list until October 22, 2025 — only after public pressure — and the full list of donors 
and their affiliations has still not been subject to meaningful independent review. 
 
This Commission, in evaluating the project, should formally request complete and independently verified 
disclosure of all funding sources, gift agreements, and any conditions or benefits attached to private 
contributions. The American people deserve to know who is paying to reshape the People’s House —  and 
why. 
 
IV. Public Accountability and Process 
 
At its core, my concern is about process — and what is lost when process is abandoned in favor of speed. 
The legally mandated review processes involving the NCPC, the Commission of Fine Arts, the National Park 
Service, and the public comment period exist for good reason. They ensure that changes to irreplaceable 
national landmarks are made deliberately, transparently, and with the benefit of expert and public input. 
They have guided White House stewardship under every administration since 1792. 
 
Those processes were bypassed here. Demolition began before plans were filed. Trees planted in honor of 
presidents Warren G. Harding and Franklin D. Roosevelt were removed without public notice. The 
Presidential Emergency Operations Center beneath the East Wing was dismantled. All of this occurred 
before this Commission had an opportunity to weigh in. 
 
I respectfully urge the National Capital Planning Commission to: 
 
Require the full scope of all planned and contemplated changes to the White House campus — including 
the West Wing colonnade addition, Lafayette Park modifications, and visitor screening changes — to be 
presented and reviewed as a comprehensive whole, not in isolated fragments. 
Condition any construction approval on complete compliance with all applicable review processes, including 
the Commission of Fine Arts and the National Environmental Policy Act, prior to further vertical 
construction. 
Mandate full public disclosure of all private funding sources, gift agreements, and donor-related conditions 
associated with this project. 
Formally recommend that appropriate congressional committees be briefed on and given the opportunity 
to weigh in on the totality of the proposed changes to the White House campus. 
Assert the Commission’s independent role free from undue influence from administration-appointed 
members who serve simultaneously on this body and in advocacy roles for the projects under review. 
 
The White House has endured for over two centuries as a symbol of democratic governance, institutional 
continuity, and the dignity of the American Republic. Its preservation is not a partisan issue. It is an 
American one. I trust this Commission to uphold that responsibility with the seriousness it deserves. 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
Angie Swenson 
Atlanta, GA

body:
The White House is a National Historic Landmark and a National Park, owned by the American people and
home to presidents since 1800. The current president at any given time is not the owner of the property or
the structures thereon; the president is a temporary tenant whose interventions are limited by law and by
respect for the people of the United States.
The demolition of the historic East Wing without review, without permits and without Congressional
oversight is clearly a violation of the law. In addition, it is a violation of the trust of the American people
who were given no opportunity to comment on what should have been presented as a proposal and not as
a violent fait accompli.
I urge the National Capital Planning Commission to require reconstruction of the East Wing in keeping with
its historic design and size. Anything constructed on the demolition site going forward must be compatible
in form and subordinate in scale to the original structure of the Executive Mansion.
The demolition of the historic East Wing without review, without permits, without effort to conserve its
materials and history, and without Congressional oversight is clearly a violation of the law.
What has happened to the historic artifacts for the East Wing, these need to be returned to the People's
House.

subject: Written Comments
name: Terry Teigen
body:
I'm a lifelong Pacific Northwest resident. I have only been in D.C. a handful of times. Once as part of a clergy
sabbatical, I was fortunnate to spend a week in the Capitol. Three mornings I got up very early, rode public
transportation, and tried to snag a tour of the White House. To no avail. It was far too popular.
When it's said the White House is "The Peoples'" it is not hyperbole or metaphor. It's a fact. Bought,
maintained, treasured by and for all of us.
Any major change to this honored part and expression of our national heritage is, of course, under the
purview of an oversight board.
It is not the property of, and should not be subject to the whims of a particular administration, and certainly
not one person. What has happened to this point is at the least a travesty and a shame. It may be far more
nefarious.
Our capitoll is not Versailles. The White House is not a castle. If someone or some group wants to build a
monument to ostentatious hubris, let them do it on their own dime, their own property, their own time.
Thank you for stopping this insult and folly.
Rev. Terry Teigen
Olympia, Washington

subject: Written Comments
name: Tina Olson
body:
I oppose the spending of $300 million on this project, which was initiated without the proper authorization,
permits, or design review. It is not a modernization project but rather a complete razing of American
history.
The White House is a National Historic Landmark and a National Park, owned by the American people and
home to presidents since 1800. The current president at any given time is not the owner of the property or
the structures thereon; the president is a temporary tenant whose interventions are limited by law and by
respect for the people of the United States.
The demolition of the historic East Wing without review, without permits and without Congressional
oversight is clearly a violation of the law. In addition, it is a violation of the trust of the American people
who were given no opportunity to comment on what should have been presented as a proposal and not as
a violent fait accompli.
I urge the National Capital Planning Commission to require reconstruction of the East Wing in keeping with
its historic design and size. Anything constructed on the demolition site going forward must be compatible
in form and subordinate in scale to the original structure of the Executive Mansion.

not just be jammed through and built without proper review and public consultation.

assessments mandated by the National Environmental Policy Act, and without congressional authorization
required by federal law for construction on federal parkland in Washington.

approving those contracts.

The White House is not private property. It belongs to the American people. No president should have
unilateral authority to demolish historic structures and approve construction without following the law and
allowing public input.
I urge the Commission to reject this proposal.
Make them build it back EXACTLY as it was.

subject: Written Comments
name: Sharon Trimber
body:
Dear Members of the Commission,
I would like to register my disapproval of the East Wing Modernization Project. As I watched the destruction
of original East Wing on various media platforms I was troubled by the lack of disregard for the history of
the building. My understanding is that in its place will be erected a ballroom financed by outside donors.
This seems to go against that the White House is the people's house. When we start to bring in outside
donors to fund a project on government property, it no longer belongs to the people. The design of the
building of the new East Wing is now determined by a select few who can now dictate and possibly redesign
and tear down any other historic buildings in the Nation's Capital. The destruction of the original East Wing
and the construction of new ballroom is a blatant disrespect for ordinary citizens to have a voice in the
process. I feel that the historical nature of the all the buildings in Washington D.C. should be taken into
consideration when deciding to take down a piece of Untied States history. It is my hope that you will
reconsider the new construction being proposed on this sight. I hope that an ordinary citizen like myself will
be heard and my input be guide for your commission. I appreciate your time and consideration and are
hopeful that this commission will make the right decision on this project.
Kind Regards,
Sharon Trimber

body:
I strongly oppose the spending of $300 million on this project, which was undertaken without proper
authorization, permits, or required design review. This is not a modernization—it is the irreversible
destruction of a significant piece of American history.
This project must be halted immediately, and the East Wing should be rebuilt and faithfully restored to its
original design. Historic preservation is not optional; it is a responsibility we owe to future generations.
No one is above the law. Allowing this project to proceed without consequences for those who ignored
legal requirements would set a dangerous precedent and erode public trust. Our laws exist to protect our
shared heritage, and they must be enforced equally and without exception.
I urge you to cancel this project and commit to restoring what has been lost.

body:
The White House is both a National Historic Landmark and a National Park, belonging to the American
people. Since 1800, it has been home to our presidents—not as owners, but as temporary caretakers
bound by law and by respect for the public trust.
Tearing down the historic East Wing without proper review, permits, or Congressional oversight is a clear
violation—not just of the law, but of the people ’s trust. This decision was made without transparency or
consent, when such a major change should have been openly proposed and carefully considered, not
executed in secret.
I urge the National Capital Planning Commission to require that the East Wing be rebuilt true to its historic
design and scale. Whatever replaces it must fit the character of the Executive Mansion—complementing,
not competing with, the original structure.

subject: Written Comments
name: Charles Ross
body:
To Whom it May Concern,
It’s important to me that historic buildings maintain their sense of character. I’m 66 years old, and I have
seen countless old buildings desecrated by modern additions out of character with the original architecture.
I have been greatly upset by the demolition of the White House East Wing. The White House is one of the
most historically important and well-recognized buildings in the country. A any external renovation project
calls for a deliberative review process with inputs – and, perhaps, veto power – from experts on historical
preservation.
The renderings I’ve seen of the new addition aren’t historically appropriate in any sense. Indeed, if the
currently-proposed building were to be constructed, the nation would need to spend additional hundreds
of millions of dollars removing it in only a few years.
Specifically, I believe that any design for the new East Wing must meet these criteria:
• Reconstruction of the East Colonnade matching its original appearance. Specifically, it should not exceed a
single story, and it should be consistent with the design for the West Colonnade.
• The main building should be no more than 1.5 stories in height, and its roof level should be lower than the
original Executive Mansion, so as not to detract from it.
• The southern end of the building should not get close to the existing curved walkway on the south lawn.
This requires a shorter building (measured north to south) and narrower building (measured east to west)
than the current proposal.
I understand that these criteria are inconsistent with the proposal for a large dining facility. So be it;
historical appropriateness is more important that the desire of ANY single president to mold the building to
his or her wishes.
Thank you for considering these inputs.
With Respect,
Charles Ross

subject: Written Comments
name: Izzy Farris
body:
I am writing to express my deep concern about the proposal to add a new ballroom to the White House. As
one of the most recognizable and historically significant buildings in the United States, the White House is
not simply a residence or event venue. It is a living symbol of our constitutional system, our shared history,
and the continuity of democratic government.
The architectural integrity of the White House has been carefully stewarded for more than two centuries.
From its original design by James Hoban to the thoughtful restorations carried out after the 1814 fire and
during the Truman renovation, changes have generally respected the building’s historic character. Adding a
large new ballroom risks shifting the balance from preservation to expansion in a way that could
permanently alter the scale, proportion, and spirit of the Executive Mansion.
While the need for event space may be cited as justification, the White House was not designed to compete
with modern convention facilities. Its power lies in its restraint, its history, and its symbolism. Major
structural additions could set a precedent that future administrations might follow, gradually transforming
a historic landmark into something more contemporary and less authentic.
I urge the National Trust to advocate strongly for preservation principles that prioritize protecting the
historic fabric, architectural coherence, and cultural meaning of the White House. Alternative solutions for
hosting large gatherings should be explored that do not compromise the integrity of this irreplaceable
building.
Thank you.

subject: Written Comments
name: Heather Joll
body:
The White House is a National Historic Landmark and a National Park owned by the American people. Since
1800, it has served not only as the residence of our presidents but as one of the most significant historic
sites in the United States. Any permanent alteration to this site warrants careful scrutiny, transparency, and
meaningful public participation.
While modernization efforts may be presented as necessary, the scale and permanence of a 90,000-square-
foot ballroom addition raise serious concerns regarding historic preservation, environmental impact, visual
integrity, long-term maintenance costs, and precedent for future alterations. The White House complex is
not merely a functional facility; it is a symbol of national heritage and continuity. Changes of this magnitude
should be evaluated not only for utility but for their effect on the historical character and symbolic
importance of the site.
This moment matters because the federal review process — including oversight by the National Capital
Planning Commission, the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, and compliance with the National Environmental
Policy Act (NEPA) — exists precisely to ensure transparency, accountability, and meaningful public input
before irreversible decisions are made. Public participation must occur before construction limits future
alternatives.
As National Trust President and CEO Carol Quillen stated, “The American people deserve an opportunity to
provide comment and shape the project.” I strongly agree. Any proposal that significantly alters a landmark
of this importance should reflect broad public consensus and careful preservation stewardship.
I respectfully urge the Commission to ensure a thorough review process, robust environmental and historic
impact analysis, and full transparency before approving any expansion of this scale.

subject: Written Comments
name: Ben Jay
body:
FORMAL OPPOSITION TO THE EAST WING MODERNIZATION PROJECT
Re: Recent Demolition and Proposed Replacement of the White House East Wing
I. Opening Statement
I write in firm and unequivocal opposition to the project known as the "East Wing Modernization," which is,
in truth, no modernization at all — but the deliberate and willful demolition of a piece of American history
that belongs not to any single administration, but to every citizen of the United States of America, and to
every generation yet to come.
This project must be stopped. Those who authorized it without legal standing must be held accountable.
And the East Wing must be fully rebuilt and restored to its former design, at the expense of those who
destroyed it.
II. This Is Not Modernization — It Is Erasure
Let us be honest about what this project actually is. The White House East Wing is a historic structure of
immense cultural, architectural, and civic significance. It has served the American people for generations —
as a workplace, a symbol, and a living piece of national heritage. To raze it in order to construct a private
ballroom, however lavishly funded, is not an act of improvement. It is an act of desecration.
A ballroom funded by tech billionaires does not belong in the White House. It belongs in a private estate, a
hotel, or a corporate campus. The people's house is not a venue for the ambitions of the ultra-wealthy. Its
architecture is not raw material for personal vanity projects. The East Wing was not theirs to touch.
III. Flagrant Violations of Law and Due Process
This project was initiated without proper authorization, without the required permits, and without the
mandatory design review processes that govern changes to historic federal structures. These are not
bureaucratic technicalities — they are legal safeguards deliberately established to protect the American
public from precisely this kind of unilateral, self-serving action.
The National Historic Preservation Act, the Preservation of Historic and Archaeological Data Act, and the
protocols of the National Trust for Historic Preservation exist for a reason. They exist because our shared
history is fragile, irreplaceable, and too important to be left to the whims of whoever happens to hold
power at a given moment. Those laws were violated. There must be consequences.
No president, no billionaire donor, no administration has the authority to unilaterally demolish a protected
historic federal structure. If this project is allowed to proceed — or worse, to be ratified after the fact — it
will set a devastating precedent: that the most powerful can simply bulldoze the law along with the
buildings.
IV. Private Funding Is Not a License to Destroy Public Property
It has been argued, or implied, that the involvement of private funding — reportedly in the range of $300
million — somehow legitimizes this project. It does not. Private money cannot purchase the right to destroy
public heritage. The White House and its historic components are the property of the American people,
held in public trust. They are not for sale, not for renovation at a donor's discretion, and not available as a
canvas for the aesthetics of whoever writes the largest check.
The appearance of private funding, in this context, does not reduce the public harm — it compounds it. It
raises serious questions about the nature of the relationship between the administration and those funding
this project, and whether the White House itself is being offered as a vehicle for their influence.
V. The National Trust for Historic Preservation Deserves Our Full Support
The National Trust for Historic Preservation has stood as a principled, courageous defender of this nation's
architectural and cultural legacy. Its intervention here is not merely procedurally appropriate — it is morally
necessary. The Trust is fighting not just for a building, but for the rule of law, for the integrity of our shared
civic institutions, and for the principle that history is not the property of the powerful.
Every American who values the preservation of our history, every citizen who believes in accountability, and
every person who understands that the law must apply equally to all — regardless of title or wealth —
should support the Trust's efforts and submit their own comment to this Commission before the March 4
deadline.
VI. Demands for Accountability and Restoration
I call upon the National Capital Planning Commission and all relevant federal authorities to take the
following actions:
1. Immediately halt and cancel the East Wing Modernization project in its entirety.
2. Require the full reconstruction and restoration of the East Wing to its original, historically accurate
design.
3. Compel those responsible for authorizing this illegal demolition to reimburse the Federal Government for
the full cost of reconstruction.
4. Initiate a full investigation into the legal violations committed in connection with this project, including
the bypassing of required permits, authorizations, and historic preservation review processes.
5. Ensure that no private funding arrangement —  past, present, or future — is permitted to override the
legal protections governing historic federal structures.
VII. Closing
No one is above the law. Not a president. Not a billionaire. Not an administration that believes its power
exempts it from the obligations every other American must meet. To allow this project to proceed
unchallenged and unpunished would be an affront to every law-abiding citizen, every taxpayer, and every
American who has ever placed their hand over their heart at the sight of the White House and felt, however
briefly, that this is the people's house.
It must be stopped. It must be reversed. And those responsible must be held accountable.
The East Wing belongs to America. Give it back.
Respectfully submitted,
Ben Jay
A Concerned American Citizen

subject: Written Comments
name: Nancy Cohen
body:
I am writing to express my concern regarding the proposed East Wing project at the White House.
The White House is not merely a functioning government building; it is a historic symbol of American
democracy with global significance. Any structural expansion or modification must therefore meet the
highest standards of transparency, preservation, and public accountability.
My concerns are as follows:
Historic Integrity: Changes to the East Wing should be evaluated carefully to ensure they do not alter the
architectural balance or diminish the historic character of the White House complex.
Transparency: Projects involving nationally significant sites warrant full public disclosure regarding scope,
cost, purpose, and long-term impact.
Precedent: Expanding federal facilities at iconic historic sites sets a precedent. Such decisions should be
undertaken only after thorough public review and expert preservation consultation.
Fiscal Responsibility: In a time of competing national priorities, it is appropriate to scrutinize the cost and
necessity of large-scale renovations or expansions.
I respectfully urge decision-makers to ensure that any changes proceed only after comprehensive public
input and preservation review.

subject: Written Comments
name: Teresa Barbee
body:
The White House, the People's House, does not need a ballroom. It is neither a hotel nor a convention
center; DC is commonplace and know for supporting conventions and meetings of various types and sizes.
There is public space available nearby (I believe it's the Commerce Building) and the central space at the
National Building Museum is huge. Union Station nearby has a lovely and large space.
The White House, the People's House, is not a Palace. It was deliberately designed and built with modest
dimensions and restrained aesthetics. Visitors to DC are often surprised at how small it is. I was surprised of
its scale when I’ve had the privilege of visiting “my house” twice in prior years. The Georgian style is
intentionally symmetrical.
The occupant of The White House is not a King; constitutionally he works for the people of the United
States and resides there as our temporary guest. The statutory guidelines, 36 CFR Part 800 prohibits and
severely restricts the ability to singularly alter a National Historic Landmark. Anyone operating in this
manner is breaking the law. He should not be able to rebuild it to his own tastes, no matter who is paying
for it.
A new East Wing should be constructed to replace the East Wing that was demolished. It should be similar
in size, shape, and placement to the West Wing, to maintain the symmetry of the entire structure. If it is
determined that the East Wing should house a ballroom, so be it--but it should be made to fit into the
original footprint and design and not of grandiose architecture and design of the exterior and interior.

name: Jerry Mitchell
body:
I don’t support the ballroom project. Washington DC has more than enough ballrooms and the concept
drawings I’ve seen appear tacky and diminish the historic landscape. I request that the East Wing be
restored, returning a look of governmental dignity to the White House. The architecture in the White House
complex is its own dignified statement about the strength of this nation. We don’t need an attempt to
compete with French, Russian, or any nations architectural heritage, and we don’t need a ballroom as a
statement about “government”.
There are compliance processes in place for historic properties in our nation and I was aghast and
disappointed that the president could take action without abiding by the laws of the nation. He’s not above
the law and it’s a bad example to the rest of the country. And there are bodies established to oversee the
stewardship of our historic heritage in DC, and the president’s vision is not more important than this
stewardship. If he thinks so, he can make his case, but the decision should not be wholly his.
Any donor dollars should be used to restore the East Wing, the historical property and landscape.

a violent fait accompli.

in form and subordinate in scale to the original structure of the Executive Mansion.

body:

ballrooms throughout the area that can host world-class events.
I work as an event producer and I know with 100% certainty that we can produce world class events in DC
for Presidents and world leaders.

subject: Written Comments
name: Kate Butt
body:
I oppose the spending of $300 million on this project, which was initiated without the proper authorization,
permits, or design review. It is not a modernization project but rather a complete razing of American
history.
The White House is a National Historic Landmark and a National Park, owned by the American people and
home to presidents since 1800. The current president at any given time is not the owner of the property or
the structures thereon; the president is a temporary tenant whose interventions are limited by law and by
respect for the people of the United States.
The demolition of the historic East Wing without review, without permits and without Congressional
oversight is clearly a violation of the law. In addition, it is a violation of the trust of the American people
who were given no opportunity to comment on what should have been presented as a proposal and not as
a violent fait accompli.
I urge the National Capital Planning Commission to require reconstruction of the East Wing in keeping with
its historic design and size. Anything constructed on the demolition site going forward must be compatible
in form and subordinate in scale to the original structure of the Executive Mansion.

subject: Written Comments
name: Michelle Budniak
body:
I respectfully submit this comment opposing the proposed ballroom addition to the White House. The
project does not comply with the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for Rehabilitation—specifically
Standards 2 and 9 (NPS Standards).
Standard 2 requires that changes avoid creating a false sense of historical development, yet the proposed
design closely replicates the White House’s neoclassical vocabulary—columns, Palladian windows, and
classical detailing—making it nearly indistinguishable from the historic structure. This approach risks
misleading the public about what is original and what is new, undermining the authenticity of one of our
nation’s most significant landmarks.
Standard 9 mandates that new additions be compatible yet clearly differentiated and visually subordinate.
The proposed ballroom fails on both counts. At approximately 90,000 square feet, it dwarfs the Executive
Residence and existing wings, disrupting the historic hierarchy. Its near-identical classical detailing provides
little visual distinction, and its placement directly attached to the East Wing makes it appear as though it
were part of the original design. Rather than complementing the historic building, the addition competes
with it, compromising its integrity.
Historic precedent demonstrates that respectful additions to the White House have always been
subordinate and clearly differentiated. Jefferson’s colonnades, Monroe’s South Portico, Jackson’s North
Portico, and the Roosevelt-era wings were purpose-built with restrained detailing and appropriate scale.
Truman’s reconstruction preserved exterior massing under strict oversight. These examples show that
additions can meet functional needs without overwhelming or falsifying history.
The proposed ballroom violates these principles and sets a troubling precedent for the stewardship of our
nation’s most iconic historic property. I urge that the project be paused and redesigned to incorporate clear
differentiation, reduce scale to ensure subordination, and undergo full review by the Commission of Fine
Arts, the National Park Service, and the Committee for the Preservation of the White House. Preserving the
integrity of the White House requires thoughtful, historically responsible design that honors its layered
history.

would like to have all construction projects proposed for the White House and White House grounds to be
reviewed by the NCPC and the CFA and comply with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), then

administrations, however, the public has a right to know project details, its impact to the existing White
House, the environment and costs. Thank you!

followed.

does not meet the Secretary of the Interiors Standards for Rehabilitation. The materials are not
appropriate.

unilateral authority to demolish historic structures and approve construction without following the law and
allowing public input.

subject: Written Comments
name: Susan Crandall
body:
Having traveled many places in the world, I have always been struck by the modesty of our White House,
that it truly was representative of leading with humility and the understanding that, while the president
lived and worked there, it was the People's House. I naturally assumed that it was in a national registry of
historical places. As with other such designated houses, it could not be altered without permission.
The fact that a president -- any president -- assumed they could make such substantive changes to our
house without going through some sort of legislative approval or even review is appalling. I was sickened
watching the demolition of the East Wing, as if our shared history had no meaning.
I deplore the idea of building up the White House into some pale variation of Versailles for one man's ego. I
lament the denigration of this monument to restrained power that, by its very modesty, emitted power --
power that did not require ostentatious display to be known.
I humbly request that something be done to put a halt to this travesty and restore the concept of the
People's House.

subject: Written Comments
name: Mary Dunbar
body:
I am a member of the National Trust for Historic Preservation (NTHP) and fully support its position with
respect to the proposed White House ballroom. The destruction of the existing East Wing without public
input was a travesty. A 90,000-square-foot ballroom is simply too big and out of scale with the rest of the
White House complex. It would overwhelm the White House itself (at 55,000 sf) and permanently ruin the
carefully balanced classical design of the White House and its two smaller, and lower, East and West Wings.
The federally recognized Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for Rehabilitation offer clear guidance for
construction projects affecting historic properties. The Standards provide that new additions should not
destroy the historic fabric of the property and that the new work should be compatible with existing
massing, size, scale, and architectural features.
The White House is owned by and belongs to the American people, not a single President, who is simply a
short-term and temporary occupant. The “taste” and preferences of a single President should not be
deciding factors. All decisions of this scale should be non-partisan and vetted by qualified independent
outside groups with historic preservation and design expertise. Any changes should respect the existing
Georgian and neoclassical design. The White House is a National Historic Landmark, a National Park, and a
globally recognized symbol of our nation’s ideals.
A new, scaled-down plan should be presented to the American people and the expert groups. Plans for the
proposed ballroom must go through the legally required public review processes, including consultation
and review by the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission of Fine Arts, with comment
from the public, and approval by Congress. These processes provide a crucial opportunity for transparency
and broad engagement, values that have guided preservation of the White House under every
administration for more than 200 years. Doing so will help ensure that the project both honors the
exceptional historic significance of the White House and acknowledges the investment that the American
people have in the preservation of this beloved place, which will go well beyond this Presidency.
Finally, there must be full transparency of any private donations. The names of the donor and the amounts
must be public along with any business they are doing before the US government.

name: Courtney Skybak
body:
The White House is owned by the American people, is a National Historic Landmark and a National Park,
and has been home to presidents since 1800. Whoever is currently president is not the owner of the
property or its structures. The president is a temporary tenant whose interventions are limited by law and
by respect for the people of the United States.
The demolition of the historic East Wing without review, without permits and without Congressional
oversight is clearly a violation of the law. It is also a violation of the trust of the American people who were
given no opportunity to comment on what should have been presented as a proposal.
I urge the National Capital Planning Commission to require reconstruction of the East Wing in keeping with
its historic design and size. Anything constructed on the demolition site going forward must be compatible
in form and subordinate in scale to the original structure of the Executive Mansion.
This has clearly never been a "modernization project" but rather a complete razing of American history. No
one is above the law and to permit this project to go ahead without penalizing those who broke the law
would be an affront to all law-abiding Americans.

subject: Written Comments
name: Mark Reber
body:
To describe this project as a "modernization" is misleading. It is no such thing. The East Wing was destroyed
in an effort to impose a ballroom described in the press as long needed and wanted. The proposed project
is far beyond the scale of the building it sits next to. At a minimum, it should be made more modest in
keeping with the other buildings that make up the White House. Further, the proposal has accelerated from
one initially described at one scale, albeit out of proportion to the rest of the White House, to an even
larger scale.
The Commission should only accept and approve a replacement for the destroyed building that maintains
the scale and is in harmony with the White House currently. Unfortunately, the destruction of the original
building places the Commission, and the American people, in an unfortunate position of having to replace,
not modernize, the East Wing.

subject: Written Comments
name: Julie JonesGoffe
body:
I am deeply opposed to spending our money (and private money) on a project that disregards our
historically legal claims to all the contents and structures that were so unceremoniously destroyed in
service of an unrealized, unconsidered concept of a plan. A symbolic bomb was detonated and needs an
equally strong response from any semblance of governmental norms and oversight we have remaining.. I
consider the action short-sighted and hope we can find a legal and moral remedy.
I firmly believe that NO permanent structure should be erected , destroyed or renamed via the whims and
winds of transitory vogue, vanity and or vulgarity of ANY administration .
We enter these public historic spaces as both guests and stewards .
I do not know the inner workings of the construction of something like The Kennedy Center but I do know
of its effect . It became a public space of creativity, a space to gather and contemporaneously honor a living
breathing history of our citizens work and art.. I would assume its construction was carefully considered. I
do not yet know the purpose of a ballroom nor any consideration given it by us. I do not know how it would
exult or benefit a citizenry or a government of and by humble people . We have not been told of its
imminent purposes that would justify the removal of "sacred" and historic relics and the destruction of
solemn and celebratory spaces. It ( the Ballroom) appears to be a thoughtless separation from our legacy
not a carefully integrated enhancement. Vulgar displays of wealth and empty ceremony has not , so far,
been our calling card or our welcome mat.
We may very well be a country that reflects more often than not a history of elite capital and commerce but
if we are going to continue to be a country of peoples with a primary place in its government we cannot
destroy their footprints at will. The artifacts and spaces where ordinary and extraordinary humans alike
have gathered is no small thing to sacrifice in favor of current private and political privilege.
Please preserve our history with the thought and care entrusted to you. Godspeed.

name: Lorie Lucky
body:
I oppose the spending of $300 million on this project, which was initiated without the proper authorization,
permits, or design review. It is not a modernization project but rather a complete razing of American
history.
The White House is a National Historic Landmark and a National Park, owned by the American people and
home to presidents since 1800. The current president at any given time is not the owner of the property or
the structures thereon; the president is a temporary tenant whose interventions are limited by law and by
respect for the people of the United States.
The demolition of the historic East Wing without review, without permits and without Congressional
oversight is clearly a violation of the law. In addition, it is a violation of the trust of the American people
who were given no opportunity to comment on what should have been presented as a proposal and not as
a violent fait accompli.
I urge the National Capital Planning Commission to require reconstruction of the East Wing in keeping with
its historic design and size. Anything constructed on the demolition site going forward must be compatible
in form and subordinate in scale to the original structure of the Executive Mansion.

subject: Written Comments
name: Terri Smith
body:
I oppose the demolition of the White House East Wing because changes to a national historic site should
occur through transparent review, not unilateral action. Additionally, this $300M project is being funded by
large private donations at the behest of the sitting administration which creates at the very least the
appearance of influence-seeking or preferential access, and undermines public trust.
The East Wing was destroyed to make way for a new state ballroom funded largely by private donors, with
demolition beginning before review by the National Capital Planning Commission and amid unresolved
preservation concerns.
I am asking for clear disclosure of donor funding, environmental and design review, and public
accountability.
The White House is a shared civic symbol, not the property of any one administration, and major alterations
should follow the same oversight standards expected of every other federally significant project.

subject: Written Comments
name: Daniel Hakala
body:
To whom it may concern,
I oppose the East Wing Modernization Project. This $400 million construction began without National
Capital Planning Commission approval, without required environmental assessments, and without
congressional authorization mandated by federal law for construction on federal parkland in Washington.
These violations should not be rewarded with after-the-fact approval.
The funding creates unacceptable conflicts of interest. Corporations holding billions in current federal
contracts with this administration are funding a construction project at the residence of the president who
controls those contracts. This is not charitable giving. This is an investment in access and favorable
treatment.
The White House belongs to the American people, not any individual president. I urge the Commission to
reject this proposal until full legal compliance is achieved, including congressional authorization and
completed environmental assessments. No temporary occupant should possess unilateral authority to
demolish historic structures without following the law.
May our voices be heard and our house preserved!
A concerned citizen of the USA,
Daniel Hakala

Ballroom will become the face of the Complex by being larger, taller, and more "out front" than the building
to which it is attached. The White House is a symbol of the President and the United States. All previous
additions have been made with careful planning so as to not take away from the original structure. Thank
you, John McDole, concerned citizen.

subject: Written Comments
name: Yvette Eastham
body:
The demolition of the East Wing, cloaked in obfuscation was a horrific tragedy. History was lost to backhoes
and wrecking balls. No review, no hearings, no public discourse occurred. Indeed the public was assured
that it was “the new ballroom project would not INTERFERE with the existing East Wing. The assurances
were misleading at best, outright lies at worst. The construction of a gargantuan ballroom as conceived by
the current occupant of The People’s House is grossly out of scale and proportion to what is left of the
Historic White House. Additionally, the price tag for this project continues to balloon. There should be
respect given to the history of the hallowed White House grounds. It is not a party venue. It is not private
property to be developed by a cadre of gold embellishing “designers”. Rather, if a venue is required of such
massive proportions for events - because clearly the other functions of the East Wing were not considered
in the demolition ie the office of the First Lady, White House Military Office, the White House visitors
entrance, the Office of Legislative Affairs, the theatre, calligraphy office, the East Collinade and the
Presidential EOC - then a formal work group should be commissioned to work with historians and architects
to design an appropriate facility. The whims of one occupant should not determine the footprint of The
People’s House. A respect and regard for history must be the focal point of any work done with The
People’s assets.

subject: Written Comments
name: Lyndele von Schill
body:
I oppose the East Wing Modernization Project. This $400 million construction began without National
Capital Planning Commission approval, without required environmental assessments, and without
congressional authorization mandated by federal law for construction on federal parkland in Washington.
These violations should not be rewarded with after-the-fact approval.
The funding creates unacceptable conflicts of interest. Corporations holding billions in current federal
contracts with this administration are funding a construction project at the residence of the president who
controls those contracts. This is not charitable giving. This is an investment in access and favorable
treatment.
The White House belongs to the American people, not any individual president. I urge the Commission to
reject this proposal until full legal compliance is achieved, including congressional authorization and
completed environmental assessments. No temporary occupant should possess unilateral authority to
demolish historic structures without following the law.

subject: Written Comments
name: Bonita Zeier
body:
I was born in Washington, DC, and attended High School 13 blocks from the White House. The challenging
world engulfing my relatives and parents, during that time in America, was brighter because I took full
advantage of the architectural spectacle that permeates the Nation's Capital. I lived weekly in the
Smithsonian complexes and visited the Capitol, White House, Memorials, and Washington Monument
often. My Mom and I have climbed the stairs in the Monument more than most in our never-ending quest
for exercise with purpose. I was absolutely CRUSHED when the East Wing of the White House was so
"unceremoniously and surprisingly" bulldozed! I thought my country "had arrived" when the Obamas
welcomed so many ordinary people into the White House. Although I didn't get to go to any of the many
functions then, I really felt (for the first time) that it was the "people's house!" It finally seemed that the
volatile roots that our Country had progressed through were mending. When I woke up on the morning that
the White House demolition happened, I immediately posted thoughts about it on Facebook and engaged
with others on my social media page. One friend wrote, "The Whitehouse hasn't seen this much destruction
since 1812." Honestly, I cried. I publish an online arts magazine, so I proceeded to gather background and
history on the gardens of the White House to post. I cried again as I highlighted changes to the gardens
made by Jacqueline Kennedy, Patricia Nixon, Michelle Obama, and Laura Bush. I couldn't believe the two
historic Magnolia Trees were deliberately destroyed -- gone. Honestly, I don't have words for how sad I felt
over this. I don't know how these losses and memories can adequately be repaired at this point. I do pray
that from this point forward, actions regarding the "People's White House" and all other historic
monuments that belong to the "People of the United States", be discussed, planned, and fully approved by
some bi-partisan committee and historical counselors before any construction ever proceeds. In fact, I think
Washington, DC should be a historic "State" where changes to any of its cultural Monuments must be
agreed upon by a contingent of counselors, including an architectural board, and no such decision should
ever be solely made by one person (not even the President).

subject: Written Comments
name: Tom St.Martin
body:
The razing and - supposed - reconstruction of the East Wing, without a public appropriation , a solid plan ,
appropriate review and approvals is an insult to me and many millions of others.
That the concept of the project appears to be nothing more than aggrandizement of the current occupant
of the White House, and a celebration of the inequality against which our ancestors rebelled, is appalling.
Since the functions it served have been relocated, I question whether it should be rebuilt at all. My
preference would be to see the wound of its former connection appropriately sealed , or at most see it
returned to some minimal, actually needed, function.
This began with the appearance of its being a vanity project. Whether true or not, that appearance casts a
shadow on the private funding of the project. To be blunt, whether it is actually so or not, it looks to many
people like an enormous attempt to curry favor. Not a good look for the government of our country, which
too many already have considered corrupt for years.
I would suggest no further work on this project until appropriately funded - i.e. transparently, publicly, via
Congressional appropriation.
I believe that was how the White House rebuild after the war of 1812 was paid for , how the Truman
reconstruction was paid for, and how the renovation of any national building should be paid for.

name: Ramona Hall
body:
I am writing to express my deep sadness and concern regarding the White House East Wing modernization.
My family and I visited the White House several years ago. I still recall the excitement and interest the 9 of
us felt as we toured the site. It remains one of my happiest memories. Yet, as I write this, I recall the
absolute gut punch of shock and sadness I experienced when I awakened to pictures of the People's House
being destroyed without notice or required approvals from various agencies. One man was allowed to
recklessly destroy a piece of our national history without facing any consequences for his actions. Thus, I
feel it is crucial that i express my deep concerns regarding the building of a new wing to the Whitehouse
that is funded by private donations and under the direction/guidance of an individual who has already
shown that he is not able to respect the history of this historic property.
I look at the changes to the Oval Office and cringe at the gaudy, fake gold wall applications that were
applied to every surface and which turned a venerated space into a gaudy Las Vegas showroom.
Furthermore, the current White House resident has never shown an ability to abide by expected norms for
historic structures. In addition to the fake gold Oval Office we also have the complete destruction of the
Lincoln bathroom. Again, slick modern surfaces with no hint of the former historic room. And I assume that
those changes were also instituted without consultation/approvals for the demolition of another historic
space.
At some point in the future, we will have to rebuild the East Wing but PLEASE consider that it must be done
by someone who has an understanding of the history of Washington, DC and of the White House and its
furnishings. Building an added structure to the White House at this time is not in the best interests of the
citizens of this country who respect our laws, regulations, and the need for historic preservation. Sincerely,

shown that he is not able to respect the history of this historic property.

space.

citizens of this country who respect our laws, regulations, and the need for historic preservation. Sincerely,

body:
NO! NO! NO! This proposed ballroom is in essence a private vanity project designed for the self-
aggrandizement of one individual. It has no place on public property, and especially not on the grounds of
the White House. The White House is not just a symbol, it is a place where the public, including visitors from
other countries have traditionally come to see, feel, and learn about what's important in our country's
history. It is a place where important diplomatic and policy discussion and decisions can be pursued and
consummated. It is NOT a party palace where glitze replaces decorum. I am personally sickened by the
destruction of the beautiful East Wing that housed and exemplefied the grace that most of our First Ladies
have brought to the Presidency. It should be restored. I am repelled by the thought of that historic East
Wing being replaced by a gilt horror of crass tastelessness, which the proposed ballroom promises to be.
One man is NOT our country and has zero right to revise its underlying values or its public symbols. There
are rules and systems. I beg you to use them to protect the people, the majority who ARE what the
government is designed to serve. Please use your power to stand for what is right NOW or the future will
never share in the awe for America that I grew up with, instead finding themselves nothing but a
maintenace mechanism for a monstrous monument to class disparities.

subject: Written Comments
name: Carol Hinchey
body:
As an American citizen, I respect and value our country’s history, and institutions. Regarding the demolition
of the East Wing of the White House, I am shocked and angry. This project was undertaken without the
requisite authorization, planning, permits and design review.
This is unacceptable. We have protocols and regulations regarding such changes and they were ignored as
we watched the destruction of an important part of American history.
Also unacceptable is the unwarranted $300 million dollar expenditure. Essential services and programs and
services have been cut or completely eliminated - to the detriment of the American people and our country
as a whole.
The only remedy for this irresponsible, disastrous and completely unnecessary action is to completely
restore the East Wing to its original state and to penalize those responsible for this unlawful action which,
in effect, is an attempt to erase and rewrite the history of our country.
Thank you for your consideration.

subject: Written Comments
name: BETTY MCNIEL
body:
Thank you for considering my comments. The White House belongs to the American People, not the
President & his donors. Please listen to us.
I oppose the spending of $300 million on this project, which was initiated without the proper authorization,
permits, or design review. It is not a modernization project but rather a complete razing of American
history.
The White House is a National Historic Landmark and a National Park, owned by the American people and
home to presidents since 1800. The current president at any given time is not the owner of the property or
the structures thereon; the president is a temporary tenant whose interventions are limited by law and by
respect for the people of the United States.
The demolition of the historic East Wing without review, without permits and without Congressional
oversight is clearly a violation of the law. In addition, it is a violation of the trust of the American people
who were given no opportunity to comment on what should have been presented as a proposal and not as
a violent fait accompli.
I urge the National Capital Planning Commission to require reconstruction of the East Wing in keeping with
its historic design and size. Anything constructed on the demolition site going forward must be compatible
in form and subordinate in scale to the original structure of the Executive Mansion.

body:
The White House is NOT a personal sandbox for a President to modify, redesign, or destroy as he sees fit.
The wrecking ball revved up without the permits and plans required before anyone can turn the East Wing
into a vanity project.
I strongly oppose any further construction of the $300+million dollar project. It should be rebuilt to be the
landmark it was that reflects the pride we used to have in our country.
